periods.activity_title: From Seed to Plate: Tracing the Grain's Journey
periods.textbook_anchor: Journey of the Grains — Observe the 12-step picture sequence and tick the elements that assist a grain in its journey (p. 88)

time_bands.activity: The teacher holds up a handful of uncooked rice or wheat grains and asks: Where did these come from before they reached your home? Students share initial ideas freely. The teacher accepts all responses and lists key words on the board — soil, rain, farmer, mill, shop — without confirming or correcting yet.

Students open Textbook p. 88 and look carefully at the 12-step picture sequence showing the grain's journey. Working individually, they tick the elements in the list — Soil, Stone, Air, Wood, Water, Tiger, Farmer, Earthworm, Hills, Fire, Insect, Bat — that actually help the grain on its way. After ticking, students compare answers with a neighbour and discuss any differences.

The teacher invites a few students to share which elements they ticked and why. As students name each helper — earthworm, farmer, water — the teacher draws out the connection: Is this helper from nature or from people? Students begin to see that both nature and humans work together. The 'Do you know?' box on harvest festivals (Textbook p. 88) is read aloud; the teacher asks which of these festivals students' families celebrate, drawing out local practices naturally.

Students write one sentence in their notebooks: name one natural helper and one human helper from the grain's journey, and say what each one does. The teacher collects a quick show of hands to check that every student has identified at least one from each group.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify natural and human contributors within an interconnected production system.
periods.section_context: 12-step picture sequence of a grain's journey; elements list: Soil, Stone, Air, Wood, Water, Tiger, Farmer, Earthworm, Hills, Fire, Insect, Bat; harvest festivals: Makar Sankranti, Akshay Tritya, Raja Utsav, Onam, Lohri.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: Could the grain reach your plate if only the farmer worked but there was no rain? This nudges students toward interdependence rather than listing contributors in isolation. If students mention a harvest festival not listed in the textbook, affirm it — local knowledge enriches the discussion.

periods.activity_title: Everyone Who Helped: Writing the Food Chain of People and Nature
periods.textbook_anchor: Journey of the Grains — Write the role of farmers in the grain's journey and list missing elements from the table (p. 88)

time_bands.activity: The teacher revisits the board words from the earlier observation activity — referring to the content of the grain's journey that students have already examined — and asks: Let's think about the farmer specifically. What exactly does the farmer do? Students respond orally.

Students open Textbook p. 88 and complete two written tasks: first, they write the farmer's role in the space provided; second, they look at the table on that page and list the elements that are missing from it. The teacher circulates, prompting students who are stuck with: Think about the pictures — what did we see happening before the grain reaches the mill?

Students turn to Textbook p. 89 and complete the 'Thank You Everyone!' activity — writing the names of all those they would like to thank for the food they eat. They may include people, animals, or elements of nature. Students then share their thank-you lists in pairs, noticing who their partner remembered that they forgot.

Each student draws a simple chain in their notebook — three to five links — showing the journey from field to plate in their own words and pictures. Below the chain, they write one sentence explaining why every link matters. The teacher moves around the room, noting the variety of chains produced.

periods.implied_lo: Students can represent the sequence of contributors in a production system through written and visual expression.
periods.section_context: Farmer's role in the grain's journey; missing elements in the journey table; 'Thank You Everyone!' gratitude activity naming people, animals, and natural elements.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt students to include contributors beyond people — earthworms, cattle, rainfall — in their thank-you lists. Ask: Is there anyone or anything we usually forget to thank? This surfaces gratitude for non-human contributors without labelling the cultural practice.

periods.activity_title: Food on My Plate: Connecting Dishes to Their Grain Ingredients
periods.textbook_anchor: Journey of the Grains — Connect the food items shown with the ingredients used to make them (p. 85)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook food items and ingredients matching activity (p. 85)

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks students: Think of the meal you had this morning. Can you name one thing you ate and what it was made from? Students share aloud. The teacher notes that many foods start as grains, and today students will trace that connection in the textbook.

Students open Textbook p. 85 and complete the matching activity — drawing lines to connect each food item shown with the ingredients (grains, pulses, vegetables) used to make it. After completing individually, students compare with a classmate sitting next to them and discuss any connections they drew differently.

The teacher leads a whole-class discussion: Which of these dishes do you eat at home? Are there dishes your family makes that use the same grain in a different way — for example, rice eaten as plain rice, as idli, or as khichdi? Students share examples from their own homes, and the teacher lists regional variations on the board, affirming that the same grain travels to very different plates.

In their notebooks, students write the name of one grain they eat often, then list two or three dishes their family makes from it. The class closes with a brief share: one student reads their list aloud, and others call out 'Same!' or a different dish they would add.

periods.implied_lo: Students can connect raw ingredients to the prepared foods made from them and relate this to their immediate food environment.
periods.section_context: Food items and grain ingredients matching activity; regional dish variations made from the same grain (rice, wheat); home food examples shared by students.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Welcome regional diversity — students from different backgrounds will name different dishes from the same grain. Ask: Does anyone's family make something with rice that your friend has never heard of? This builds the near-to-far principle through peer sharing.

periods.activity_title: Eating with Full Attention: The Mindful Peanut Experience
periods.textbook_anchor: Mindful Eating — Guided sensory eating experience with a peanut, attending to touch, taste, smell, and texture (p. 92)

time_bands.activity: Each student receives one peanut. The teacher asks students to close their eyes and simply hold it for a moment — not to eat it yet. What does it feel like in your hand? Rough, smooth, light, heavy? Students whisper their observations.

The teacher guides the class through the mindful eating activity described in Textbook p. 92: students keep their eyes closed, bring the peanut to their nose, then slowly place it in their mouths without chewing — noticing the taste, texture, and any saliva response. They then chew very slowly, paying attention to how the texture changes and what flavours emerge. The teacher speaks slowly and leaves pauses, mirroring the classroom narrative in the textbook.

Students open their eyes and discuss in small groups: What did your tongue notice? What did your teeth do? What happened to the food inside your mouth as you chewed slowly? Each group nominates one speaker to share with the class. The teacher records key sense-words on the board.

Students write three sentences in their notebooks — one for each discussion question on Textbook p. 92 — describing the role of the tongue, the teeth, and the changes inside the mouth. The teacher checks that students are writing from their own experience, not copying.

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe sensory observations made during a structured food-tasting experience and connect them to how the body processes food.
periods.section_context: Mindful eating guided experience with a peanut; sensory roles of tongue, teeth, and mouth; slow eating and attention to taste, texture, smell.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Keep the guided eating phase genuinely slow and unhurried — resist the impulse to move on when students laugh or fidget. Ask: Was eating this peanut different from how you normally eat? That question bridges the experience to the habit.

periods.activity_title: A Week of Watching What I Eat: The Food Diary
periods.textbook_anchor: Valuing Food — Record food eaten for breakfast, lunch, and dinner over a week, noting whether food was finished or wasted (p. 93)

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: Has anyone here ever left food on their plate? Why? Students respond honestly. The teacher then asks: Do you know how far that grain travelled to reach your plate? Students briefly recall the journey they traced — from field to farm to mill to shop to kitchen — to anchor the value of not wasting.

Students open Textbook p. 93 and study the food diary table. The teacher walks through the columns — day, meal, what was eaten, whether it was finished — and explains the smiley/sad-face coding system. Students set up the same table in their notebooks, copying the headings. Together the class fills in today's entry as a shared practice run, with students calling out what they had for breakfast this morning.

The teacher leads a discussion: What do we do when someone puts more food on our plate than we can eat (Textbook p. 93)? What do we do when there is something on our plate we dislike? Students discuss in pairs, then share responses. The teacher lists agreed strategies on the board — politely say 'just a little', try a small bite, not leave it untouched.

Students write their answers to the two 'Write' prompts on Textbook p. 93 — what they would do if offered too much food, and what they would do if they dislike a food item. The teacher reminds students that the diary is a personal record they will fill at home each day for the week ahead, bringing the completed table back when class next meets this section's content.

periods.implied_lo: Students can plan and carry out a structured self-observation record of their own food consumption and reflect on food-wasting behaviour.
periods.section_context: Seven-day food diary table for breakfast, lunch, and dinner; smiley/sad-face coding for food finished or wasted; written responses on handling excess food and disliked food.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Emphasise that the diary is not about eating 'correctly' but about noticing honestly. Ask: What would you feel if you knew the farmer worked all season for that grain you left on your plate? This connects valuing food to the journey already studied.

periods.activity_title: Every Grain Counts: Reflecting on Food Diaries and Sharing Strategies
periods.textbook_anchor: Valuing Food — Reflect on food consumption record and write responses to situations involving excess or disliked food (p. 93)

time_bands.activity: Students who have kept their food diaries share one interesting thing they noticed — a day they ate everything, a day they wasted something, or a food they were surprised to enjoy. The teacher accepts all observations without judgment, noting that honest noticing is the point of the diary.

In small groups, students share their food diary tables and look for patterns: On which days did they finish their food? On which days did they leave something? Did anyone waste more at a particular meal? Groups appoint a reporter who summarises the group's findings for the class. The teacher listens and draws out the idea that habits across the week are more revealing than a single day.

The teacher reopens the two written prompts from Textbook p. 93 — excess food and disliked food — and invites students to share the strategies they wrote. The class builds a shared list of respectful, waste-reducing responses. The teacher asks: Are any of these things your family already does? This draws out household food values and traditional practices around not wasting.

Each student writes one personal commitment in their notebook: one specific change they will make in how they handle food at home, and why it matters. A few students share their commitment aloud. The teacher affirms the diversity of commitments — reducing waste looks different in different homes.

periods.implied_lo: Students can analyse their own food-consumption patterns from recorded data and articulate strategies for reducing food waste.
periods.section_context: Food diary data review across a week; group pattern analysis of finished versus wasted meals; strategies for handling excess food and disliked food; personal waste-reduction commitments.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Avoid shaming students whose diaries show waste — focus the discussion on what they noticed and what they could try differently. Ask: What made it hard to finish your food on some days? This opens structural factors (portion size, food preferences, being served by others) without blame.

periods.activity_title: Spot the Sport: Identifying Physical Activities in a Park Scene
periods.textbook_anchor: Enjoy Sports — Identify the activities people are engaged in from the park picture (p. 94)

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: What did you do after school yesterday? Were you running, cycling, playing, or sitting? Students share quickly. The teacher notes that physical activity is not just sport — it includes everything that gets the body moving — and today the class will look carefully at a busy park to see how many activities they can find.

Students open Textbook p. 94 and study the park scene picture carefully. Individually, they list in their notebooks all the activities they can identify — naming each one specifically (skipping, running, cycling, etc.) rather than just writing 'playing'. They then count how many different activities they found.

The teacher invites students to share their lists. As each activity is named, the teacher asks: Have you ever done this? How did your body feel while doing it? The class also discusses which activities from the picture they do in their own daily lives (Textbook p. 95 discussion prompts). Students note the difference between activities they do and those they have never tried.

Students write two or three sentences answering: Which physical activities do you do in your daily life, and how do you feel on a day when you play a lot? They draw a quick stick figure doing their favourite physical activity beside their writing. A few students share.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify and describe a range of physical activities from visual observation and connect them to their own daily experience.
periods.section_context: Park scene showing diverse sports and playground activities; student identification of running, cycling, skipping, jumping, and other activities; reflection on personal daily physical activity and how it feels.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: Are there activities in the picture that you do not see in your neighbourhood? This gently moves students from the local to the wider world. Affirm all forms of physical activity — including traditional play that students may mention — as equally valuable.

periods.activity_title: Traditional Games and Yoga: Finding Out and Trying Out
periods.textbook_anchor: Enjoy Sports — Practice easy yoga poses and record observations over a week (p. 95)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook yoga pose illustrations and traditional games pictures (p. 95)

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 95 and look at the pictures of traditional games. Working in pairs, they try to name each game depicted. The teacher asks: Has anyone played any of these games? Where did you learn it? Students share briefly; the teacher notes that many of these games have been played by children in India across many generations.

The teacher guides the class through the easy yoga poses shown in Textbook p. 95. Students try each pose where they stand, with the teacher checking posture gently. The teacher introduces the observation record from the textbook activity — students are to practise these poses at home over the coming days and record how they feel each day. In class, students set up the observation table in their notebooks now, so they are ready to begin recording.

Students reflect and discuss in small groups: How did your body feel when you tried the yoga pose just now — steady, wobbly, stretched? What do you think regular practice might do? Groups share one observation each. The teacher connects this to the textbook's statement that yoga improves posture and keeps one happy and active.

Each student writes in their notebook: the name of one traditional game from the textbook pictures they want to learn, and one yoga pose they will practise. Below, they write one prediction: what do they think will change if they practise the pose every day for a week? This becomes the start of their inquiry record.

periods.implied_lo: Students can carry out a structured observation inquiry by practising a physical activity over time and recording how their body feels.
periods.section_context: Traditional Indian games depicted in textbook pictures; easy yoga poses from Textbook p. 95; observation record table for week-long yoga practice; student predictions about regular practice.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: When students name traditional games, ask: Did anyone learn this from a grandparent or older relative? This surfaces intergenerational knowledge without labelling it. Ensure every student has their observation table set up before the unit closes.

periods.activity_title: Sleep Matters: Recording Rest and Noticing How I Feel
periods.textbook_anchor: Sleep Well too! — Fill the sleep record table noting sleep time, wake time, duration, and how you felt the next day (p. 97)

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: Raise your hand if you felt fresh and alert this morning. Now raise your hand if you felt tired or sleepy. What do you think made the difference? Students share briefly. The teacher introduces the idea that sleep is the third pillar of healthy living alongside eating and exercising, and today the class will learn to track it.

Students open Textbook p. 97 and study the sleep record table. The teacher explains each column: when they slept, when they got up, how long they slept, and how they felt — using the key: a = felt fresh, b = lazy, c = sleepy. Students copy the table into their notebooks and fill in last night's data from memory as a practice entry.

Students discuss in pairs the two discussion questions on Textbook p. 97: Why does our body need rest? Is it important to rest after a busy day of exercise and play? Partners take turns explaining their thinking. The teacher then invites one or two pairs to share their reasoning with the class, and adds any key ideas students miss — such as the body repairing itself during sleep.

Students write their answers to both discussion questions in their notebooks as short paragraphs. The teacher reminds students to keep adding to their sleep tables at home for the next two days, so they have a three-day record. Each student writes the three-day recording task as a reminder in their notebook.

periods.implied_lo: Students can record and interpret personal sleep data and reason about why rest is necessary for the body.
periods.section_context: Sleep record table with columns for sleep time, wake time, duration, and next-day feeling (fresh/lazy/sleepy); body's need for rest; rest after exercise and play.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Avoid asking students to share exact sleep times publicly if some children have irregular schedules due to household circumstances. Frame the discussion around what students noticed about the connection between sleep and how they felt, not on judging sleep duration.

periods.activity_title: Rested or Tired? Discussing What Our Sleep Data Tells Us
periods.textbook_anchor: Sleep Well too! — Discuss why the body needs rest and whether rest after exercise and play is important (p. 97)

time_bands.activity: Students refer to the sleep record tables they have been filling at home. The teacher asks: Look at your three days — did the amount of sleep you got change how you felt the next day? Students examine their own tables quietly before discussing.

In small groups, students compare their three-day sleep records. They look for a pattern: on days they slept for what felt like a long stretch, did they tend to mark 'a' (fresh) more often? On shorter nights, did they mark 'b' or 'c'? Each group prepares one sentence summarising their group's pattern to share with the class.

Groups share their summaries. The teacher brings the discussion back to the two questions on Textbook p. 97 — body's need for rest, and rest after exercise — building on what students discovered from their own data. The teacher introduces the three-pillar summary: eating right, exercising, and sleeping well all work together.

Students write a short reflection in their notebooks: What is one thing their sleep record showed them that surprised them, and one change they could make to sleep better? A few students share. The teacher closes by affirming that noticing our own body's signals is a skill worth keeping.

periods.implied_lo: Students can draw a conclusion from their own recorded sleep data and connect adequate rest to overall well-being.
periods.section_context: Three-day sleep record data — sleep time, wake time, duration, and next-day feeling; group pattern analysis of sleep and freshness; three pillars of healthy living: eating, exercising, sleeping.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: Did anyone find that a day with lots of play also meant they slept better that night? This links the Enjoy Sports content students already experienced to sleep. Keep the discussion grounded in students' own data.

periods.activity_title: Safe and Unsafe Touch: Sorting Situations and Naming Our Feelings
periods.textbook_anchor: Feeling Safe — Look at pictures of different situations and tick comfortable or cross uncomfortable (p. 98)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook pictures of safe and unsafe situations (p. 98)

time_bands.activity: The teacher introduces this unit with a calm, matter-of-fact tone: Today we are going to talk about something important — how our body tells us when we feel safe and when we do not. The teacher establishes that this is a safe space and all answers are accepted. Students are told there are no wrong feelings.

Students open Textbook p. 98 and look at the pictures of different situations carefully. For each picture, they put a tick where the child in the picture would feel comfortable and a cross where the child would feel uncomfortable. Students work individually and quietly. The teacher moves around the room without rushing students.

The teacher reviews the pictures one by one with the class, asking: What did you notice in this picture that made you choose a tick or a cross? Students share their observations. The teacher draws out the key distinction: a safe touch is one that makes you feel cared for; an unsafe touch is one that makes you feel uneasy, scared, or confused — and it does not matter whether the person is known or a stranger.

Students write two or three sentences in their notebooks describing in their own words what makes a touch safe and what makes it unsafe. The teacher reads a few aloud (without naming the student) to affirm correct understanding and gently correct any confusion.

periods.implied_lo: Students can classify physical interactions as safe or unsafe based on how the body and feelings respond.
periods.section_context: Textbook pictures of safe and unsafe touch situations; tick/cross classification activity; distinction between safe touch (caring, comfortable) and unsafe touch (uneasy, scared, confused, known or stranger).
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Keep the tone calm and factual throughout — children should feel empowered, not frightened. If a student seems distressed, check in quietly after the unit. Avoid singling out any student's personal experience in the group discussion.

periods.activity_title: My Voice, My Safety: Saying No and Telling a Trusted Adult
periods.textbook_anchor: Feeling Safe — Write what you would do if a touch made you uncomfortable, who you would tell, and two situations where you would say No (p. 99)

time_bands.activity: The teacher begins: We have seen that our body tells us when something feels wrong. Today we think about what we can DO when that happens. The teacher lists the three actions on the board: Say No firmly, walk away, and tell a trusted adult. Students discuss briefly: Who would be a trusted adult for them — a parent, a teacher, a relative?

Students open Textbook p. 99 and complete the three written tasks: what they would do if a touch made them uncomfortable; who they would tell in an unsafe situation; and two situations where they would firmly say 'No'. The teacher circulates and reads responses privately, affirming students who name concrete trusted adults and specific situations.

The teacher leads a brief whole-class discussion using fictional scenarios (not personal ones): 'Imagine a child at a bus stop feels someone touching their shoulder in a way that makes them uncomfortable. What should that child do?' Students walk through the three steps together. The teacher emphasises: saying 'No' is always allowed, and a trusted adult will always believe you and help.

Students write one personal statement in their notebooks: 'I have the right to feel safe, and if I feel unsafe I will...' and complete it in their own words. A few students share their completions. The teacher affirms each response and closes with a reminder that speaking up is a sign of strength.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify appropriate responses to unsafe situations and articulate the right to bodily safety.
periods.section_context: Written responses to unsafe touch: what to do, who to tell, two situations to say No; three-step response: say No, walk away, tell a trusted adult; right to safety and speaking up.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Use only fictional or general scenarios in class discussion — never ask students to share personal experiences of unsafe situations in a group. Remind students privately that you are always available to talk. This unit's value lies in students leaving with a clear plan, not in emotional processing as a group.

periods.activity_title: What If It Was Missing? Reasoning About the Food Chain
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Write what would happen to a food grain if each element (soil, water, sunlight, cattle, earthworm, farmer, shopkeeper, cook) were missing (p. 100)

time_bands.activity: The teacher poses a riddle: A grain of rice is trying to reach your plate, but today the farmer did not go to the field. What happens? Students respond. The teacher then asks: What if it was the earthworm that was missing? The cook? Students begin to see that each element plays an irreplaceable role.

Students open Textbook p. 100 and work on the reflection task: for each element listed — Soil, Water, Sunlight, Cattle, Earthworm, Farmer, Shopkeeper, Cook — they write what would happen to the grain's journey if that element were absent. Students work individually, writing one sentence per element.

Students share their reasoning in pairs, comparing what they wrote for the same element. The teacher then invites the class to discuss: Are some elements more essential than others, or does removing any one of them break the whole journey? Students argue both sides respectfully. The teacher does not give a definitive answer, keeping the reasoning open.

Students write a closing statement in their notebooks: 'The journey of a grain depends on... because...' using at least three elements in their explanation. A few students read their statements aloud. The teacher notes the quality of reasoning — are students giving causes, not just naming the missing element?

periods.implied_lo: Students can reason about the consequence of removing one contributor from an interdependent system and justify their thinking.
periods.section_context: Consequence reasoning for missing elements: Soil, Water, Sunlight, Cattle, Earthworm, Farmer, Shopkeeper, Cook; interdependence of all contributors in the grain's journey.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Push students beyond 'the grain would die' to more specific reasoning — without soil, the seed cannot germinate; without the cook, the grain cannot become a meal. Ask: What exactly stops happening when this one thing is missing? Precision of reasoning is the goal here.

periods.activity_title: My Balanced Plate: Designing Breakfast, Lunch, and Dinner
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Design your own favourite plate of balanced diet for breakfast, lunch, and dinner without wasting food (p. 100)

time_bands.activity: The teacher asks: If you could design your own perfect breakfast, lunch, and dinner plate — and it had to be balanced and leave nothing wasted — what would you put on it? Students share their first ideas aloud. The teacher notes a few on the board and asks: What does 'balanced' mean to you?

Students open Textbook p. 100 and begin the design task: they draw three circles (or use three sections in their notebook) labelled Breakfast, Lunch, and Dinner. Inside each, they draw and label the food items they would include, choosing foods they genuinely like that together form a balanced meal. Beside each plate, they write a brief note explaining why they chose those items and how they will make sure nothing is wasted.

Students share their plates in small groups. Each student explains one choice they made — why they included a particular food or how they planned to avoid waste. Peers ask one question about each plate. The teacher circulates, listening for the connection between balanced eating and the valuing-food ideas encountered earlier in the chapter.

Students write one sentence under their three plates: 'I chose these foods because...' — linking their design to what they know about balanced eating and not wasting food. A few plates are shared with the whole class.

periods.implied_lo: Students can design a balanced meal plan that reflects understanding of nutritional variety and food-waste reduction.
periods.section_context: Design task: breakfast plate, lunch plate, dinner plate with balanced food items chosen by the student; written justification for food choices; connection to no-waste principle.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Affirm regional and cultural variety in plate designs — a student whose plate features local foods from their region is demonstrating exactly the right thinking. Ask: How do you make sure you finish everything on this plate? This connects the design task to the valuing-food commitment.

periods.activity_title: My Well-being Plan: Habits for a Happy, Healthy Life
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Indicate your plans for daily habits: wake up early, yoga and exercises, eat a balanced diet on time, exercise and play, less use of TV and mobile, read a book, sleep peacefully (p. 101)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens with a quiet moment: Think about a day when you felt really good — energetic, happy, and calm. What had you done that day? Students share briefly. The teacher notes patterns on the board — often such days involve eating well, playing, and sleeping enough — and introduces the idea that these can become deliberate habits.

Students open Textbook p. 101 and study the habit planning table listing: Wake up early, Yoga and exercises, Eat a balanced diet on time, Exercise and play, Less use of TV and mobile, Read a book, Sleep peacefully. For each habit, students indicate their personal plan — how they will make this a regular part of their day — in their notebooks. They also respond to the reflection prompts on Textbook p. 101 about mindful eating experiences and exercises they enjoy.

Students share their habit plans in pairs, explaining which habit they think will be easiest to keep and which will be hardest, and why. The teacher then invites the class to think about which of these habits also help others — eating without wasting, for example, or spending less time on screens and more time playing with friends.

Each student creates a short personal well-being pledge in their notebook — choosing three habits from the list and writing why each one matters to them. Students may decorate their pledge. A few students read their pledges aloud. The teacher closes by affirming that small, consistent habits are what build a healthy and happy life.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify and commit to specific personal habits that support physical and emotional well-being.
periods.section_context: Daily habit planning table: Wake up early, Yoga and exercises, Eat a balanced diet on time, Exercise and play, Less use of TV and mobile, Read a book, Sleep peacefully; mindful eating reflection; exercises and games enjoyed; personal well-being pledge.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Let students choose which three habits to pledge — do not prescribe. Ask: Which of these habits have you already been trying since we started this chapter? This connects the pledge to the food diary, sleep record, and yoga practice students have already experienced, through the content rather than by naming any unit.

coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students observe the 12-step grain journey picture sequence and tick which listed elements (natural and human) assist the grain, then discuss the connection between nature and people in food production.

coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students write the farmer's role, identify missing elements, complete the Thank You Everyone activity, and create a personal drawn chain showing the grain's journey from field to plate.

coverage_handoff.section_context: Food items and grain ingredients matching activity; regional dish variations made from the same grain (rice, wheat); home food examples shared by students.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Journey of the Grains — Connect the food items shown with the ingredients used to make them (p. 85)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students match food items to their grain ingredients in the textbook, then discuss regional dish variations made from the same grain and record their own family's grain-based dishes.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can describe sensory observations made during a structured food-tasting experience and connect them to how the body processes food.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Mindful eating guided experience with a peanut; sensory roles of tongue, teeth, and mouth; slow eating and attention to taste, texture, smell.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Mindful Eating — Guided sensory eating experience with a peanut, attending to touch, taste, smell, and texture (p. 92)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students carry out the guided mindful peanut-eating experience, then discuss and write about the roles of the tongue, teeth, and mouth sensed during slow, attentive eating.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can plan and carry out a structured self-observation record of their own food consumption and reflect on food-wasting behaviour.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Seven-day food diary table for breakfast, lunch, and dinner; smiley/sad-face coding for food finished or wasted; written responses on handling excess food and disliked food.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Valuing Food — Record food eaten for breakfast, lunch, and dinner over a week, noting whether food was finished or wasted (p. 93)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students set up and begin the seven-day food diary, practise filling today's entry together, and write responses to the textbook prompts about handling excess and disliked food.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can analyse their own food-consumption patterns from recorded data and articulate strategies for reducing food waste.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Food diary data review across a week; group pattern analysis of finished versus wasted meals; strategies for handling excess food and disliked food; personal waste-reduction commitments.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Valuing Food — Reflect on food consumption record and write responses to situations involving excess or disliked food (p. 93)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students review their completed food diary data in groups, identify patterns of food waste or completion, share and discuss waste-reduction strategies, and write a personal food commitment.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can identify and describe a range of physical activities from visual observation and connect them to their own daily experience.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Park scene showing diverse sports and playground activities; student identification of running, cycling, skipping, jumping, and other activities; reflection on personal daily physical activity and how it feels.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Enjoy Sports — Identify the activities people are engaged in from the park picture (p. 94)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students observe the textbook park scene and list all physical activities they can identify, then discuss which they do daily and write about how physical activity makes them feel.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can carry out a structured observation inquiry by practising a physical activity over time and recording how their body feels.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Traditional Indian games depicted in textbook pictures; easy yoga poses from Textbook p. 95; observation record table for week-long yoga practice; student predictions about regular practice.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Enjoy Sports — Practice easy yoga poses and record observations over a week (p. 95)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students try to name traditional games from textbook pictures, practise easy yoga poses in class, set up a week-long observation record table, and write a prediction about the effect of regular practice.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can record and interpret personal sleep data and reason about why rest is necessary for the body.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Sleep record table with columns for sleep time, wake time, duration, and next-day feeling (fresh/lazy/sleepy); body's need for rest; rest after exercise and play.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Sleep Well too! — Fill the sleep record table noting sleep time, wake time, duration, and how you felt the next day (p. 97)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students set up the three-day sleep record table and fill in a practice entry, then discuss and write answers to the textbook questions about why the body needs rest and rest after exercise.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can draw a conclusion from their own recorded sleep data and connect adequate rest to overall well-being.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Three-day sleep record data — sleep time, wake time, duration, and next-day feeling; group pattern analysis of sleep and freshness; three pillars of healthy living: eating, exercising, sleeping.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Sleep Well too! — Discuss why the body needs rest and whether rest after exercise and play is important (p. 97)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students review their three-day sleep records in groups, identify patterns linking sleep duration to next-day feeling, and write a personal reflection on what their sleep data revealed.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can classify physical interactions as safe or unsafe based on how the body and feelings respond.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Textbook pictures of safe and unsafe touch situations; tick/cross classification activity; distinction between safe touch (caring, comfortable) and unsafe touch (uneasy, scared, confused, known or stranger).
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Feeling Safe — Look at pictures of different situations and tick comfortable or cross uncomfortable (p. 98)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students examine textbook pictures of various situations, classify each as comfortable or uncomfortable, discuss the defining features of safe versus unsafe touch, and write their own description of the distinction.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can identify appropriate responses to unsafe situations and articulate the right to bodily safety.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Written responses to unsafe touch: what to do, who to tell, two situations to say No; three-step response: say No, walk away, tell a trusted adult; right to safety and speaking up.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Feeling Safe — Write what you would do if a touch made you uncomfortable, who you would tell, and two situations where you would say No (p. 99)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students write their three responses to unsafe touch scenarios in the textbook, practise the three-step response using a fictional scenario, and compose a personal safety statement.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can reason about the consequence of removing one contributor from an interdependent system and justify their thinking.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Consequence reasoning for missing elements: Soil, Water, Sunlight, Cattle, Earthworm, Farmer, Shopkeeper, Cook; interdependence of all contributors in the grain's journey.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Write what would happen to a food grain if each element (soil, water, sunlight, cattle, earthworm, farmer, shopkeeper, cook) were missing (p. 100)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students reason and write about what would happen to a grain's journey if each listed contributor were absent, then debate whether any single element is more essential than others.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can design a balanced meal plan that reflects understanding of nutritional variety and food-waste reduction.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Design task: breakfast plate, lunch plate, dinner plate with balanced food items chosen by the student; written justification for food choices; connection to no-waste principle.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Design your own favourite plate of balanced diet for breakfast, lunch, and dinner without wasting food (p. 100)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students draw and label three balanced meal plates for breakfast, lunch, and dinner, write justifications for their food choices, and share their designs in small groups.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can identify and commit to specific personal habits that support physical and emotional well-being.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Daily habit planning table: Wake up early, Yoga and exercises, Eat a balanced diet on time, Exercise and play, Less use of TV and mobile, Read a book, Sleep peacefully; mindful eating reflection; exercises and games enjoyed; personal well-being pledge.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Indicate your plans for daily habits: wake up early, yoga and exercises, eat a balanced diet on time, exercise and play, less use of TV and mobile, read a book, sleep peacefully (p. 101)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students complete the habit planning table in the textbook, write reflections on mindful eating and physical activities enjoyed, and create a personal well-being pledge committing to three chosen daily habits.

assessment_items.question_text: A grain of rice needs many helpers to reach your plate. Which of the following is a NATURAL helper in the grain's journey?

options.label: A
options.text: Cook

options.label: B
options.text: Earthworm

options.label: C
options.text: Mill worker

options.label: D
options.text: Shopkeeper

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer: C. The earthworm is a natural helper that improves soil quality. All other options are human contributors to the journey.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify natural and human contributors within an interconnected production system.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing 'Mill worker' shows the student has identified a real contributor but confused a human agent with a natural one — they may not yet distinguish the two categories.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing 'Shopkeeper' shows the student recognises a step in the journey but cannot distinguish human from natural helpers.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 'Cook' shows the student knows the cook is part of the journey but has not grasped the natural/human distinction.

assessment_items.question_text: Look at the journey of a grain from field to plate. Choose ONE person who helps along the way and explain what would be different about your meal if that person did not do their work.
expected_elements: Names a specific human contributor from the grain's journey (farmer, mill worker, shopkeeper, or cook).
Describes the specific role that person plays in the journey.
Explains a specific consequence for the meal if that person were absent.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any human contributor named in the chapter. The key quality indicator is whether the student links the person's absence to a specific consequence (e.g. without the mill worker, the grain cannot be ground into flour). Credit any reasonable consequence that follows logically.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can represent the sequence of contributors in a production system through written and visual expression.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

expected_elements: Names a specific human contributor from the grain's journey (farmer, mill worker, shopkeeper, or cook).
Describes the specific role that person plays in the journey.
Explains a specific consequence for the meal if that person were absent.

assessment_items.question_text: Priya's family eats idli for breakfast and chapati for dinner. Both dishes come from grains. Which statement best explains this?

options.label: A
options.text: Chapati is made from rice and idli is made from wheat.

options.label: B
options.text: Different grains can be used to make different foods that families eat.

options.label: C
options.text: Idli and chapati are made from the same grain.

options.label: D
options.text: Only rice can be used to make breakfast foods.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer: B. Idli is typically made from rice and urad dal; chapati is made from wheat flour. The item tests whether students understand that the same chapter's grain concept applies across different foods and regional practices. Regional variation note: accept any locally appropriate example a student provides in a follow-up discussion, as grain-to-dish relationships vary by region.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can connect raw ingredients to the prepared foods made from them and relate this to their immediate food environment.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing 'same grain' shows the student has not distinguished the two grains covered in the chapter — a confusion between rice and wheat.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing 'only rice for breakfast' shows an overgeneralisation from a single regional example, missing the diversity of grain-to-dish connections.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option shows the student has the grains reversed — a specific factual misconception about which grain produces which dish.

assessment_items.question_text: During the mindful peanut-eating activity, Rehan noticed something new about how his mouth works. Describe TWO things that happen inside the mouth when food is eaten slowly and carefully.
expected_elements: Describes the role of the tongue (sensing taste, moving food, feeling texture).
Describes the role of the teeth (chewing, breaking food into smaller pieces).
OR describes a change that happens to the food inside the mouth (texture changes, mixing with saliva, food becoming soft).
assessment_items.annotation: Award credit for any two of the three expected elements. The student must describe an observable process, not simply name a body part.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe sensory observations made during a structured food-tasting experience and connect them to how the body processes food.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

expected_elements: Describes the role of the tongue (sensing taste, moving food, feeling texture).
Describes the role of the teeth (chewing, breaking food into smaller pieces).
OR describes a change that happens to the food inside the mouth (texture changes, mixing with saliva, food becoming soft).

assessment_items.question_text: Sana is keeping a food diary for a week. On Tuesday, she ate only half her lunch and left the rest. What should she write in her diary for Tuesday's lunch?

options.label: A
options.text: Leave that row blank because she did eat something.

options.label: B
options.text: Write 'No' and draw a sad face.

options.label: C
options.text: Write 'Yes' and draw a happy smiley.

options.label: D
options.text: Write 'Yes' because she ate more than half her food.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer: B. The food diary coding in the textbook is clear: if food was left, write 'No' and draw a sad face. The item tests whether students understood the diary's purpose as an honest record, not a positive self-report.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can plan and carry out a structured self-observation record of their own food consumption and reflect on food-wasting behaviour.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing 'Yes with smiley' shows the student missed or misread the coding system — they may be recording how they feel generally rather than whether they finished the food.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 'Leave blank' shows the student does not understand that partial eating is a meaningful data point in the inquiry.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing 'Yes because she ate more than half' shows the student is applying a proportion-based rule not stated in the textbook — a logical but incorrect inference.

assessment_items.question_text: After keeping her food diary for a week, Maya noticed she wasted food more often at dinner than at breakfast. What does this pattern tell her, and what is ONE thing she could change at dinner time to waste less food?
look_for: Interprets the pattern meaningfully — e.g. recognises that dinner portions may be too large, or that by evening she is less hungry.
Connects the pattern to a specific, practical change at dinner time (e.g. taking a smaller portion, telling the person serving to give less, choosing foods she likes).
Shows awareness that wasting food disrespects the effort of those who produced it, or that every grain has value.
assessment_items.annotation: A strong response identifies a plausible reason for the pattern and proposes a concrete, actionable change. Credit any culturally appropriate dinner-time strategy. Partial credit for responses that only describe the pattern without proposing a change.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can analyse their own food-consumption patterns from recorded data and articulate strategies for reducing food waste.

competency.competency_text: Learns about basic social and behavioural norms, values, and dispositions that benefit our social and natural environments and that help our society function smoothly (using dustbins, standing in queues, conserving water, using public transportation, keeping one's environment clean, always helping others in need regardless of background)

look_for: Interprets the pattern meaningfully — e.g. recognises that dinner portions may be too large, or that by evening she is less hungry.
Connects the pattern to a specific, practical change at dinner time (e.g. taking a smaller portion, telling the person serving to give less, choosing foods she likes).
Shows awareness that wasting food disrespects the effort of those who produced it, or that every grain has value.

assessment_items.question_text: Rohan looked at a picture of a park and found children running, skipping, cycling, and playing on swings. What do ALL of these activities have in common?

options.label: A
options.text: They all get the body moving and keep it strong and energetic.

options.label: B
options.text: They all need special equipment that must be bought.

options.label: C
options.text: They are only for children who are already very fit.

options.label: D
options.text: They can only be done in a park.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer: B. The section emphasises that all physical activity — regardless of type or equipment — keeps the body strong and energetic. Distractors probe misconceptions about accessibility and location.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify and describe a range of physical activities from visual observation and connect them to their own daily experience.

competency.competency_text: Describes the basic safety needs and protection (health and hygiene, food, water, shelter, precautions, awareness of emergency situations, abuse, and unsafe situations) of humans, birds, and animals

what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing 'special equipment' shows the student has overgeneralised from activities that do need equipment (cycling) to all activities — a within-chapter confusion.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing 'only in a park' shows the student has anchored the activity to the textbook's park picture rather than the generalised concept of physical activity.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing 'only for fit children' shows a misconception about inclusivity — the section presents physical activity as accessible to all children.

assessment_items.question_text: Aisha tried a yoga pose in class and then planned to practise it every day for a week. She decided to write down how her body felt each day. Why is it important to record observations every day rather than just trying to remember at the end of the week?
expected_elements: States that daily recording captures accurate, day-by-day details that are hard to remember later.
Explains that noticing changes each day helps identify a pattern or trend over time.
Connects the record to making a reliable conclusion about the effect of regular practice.
assessment_items.annotation: A complete response addresses accuracy of daily recording and its value for identifying patterns. Two of the three expected elements are sufficient for full credit.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can carry out a structured observation inquiry by practising a physical activity over time and recording how their body feels.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: States that daily recording captures accurate, day-by-day details that are hard to remember later.
Explains that noticing changes each day helps identify a pattern or trend over time.
Connects the record to making a reliable conclusion about the effect of regular practice.

assessment_items.question_text: Dev filled in his sleep record table for three days. On Day 1 he slept for a short stretch and marked 'c' (sleepy) the next day. On Day 2 he slept for a long stretch and marked 'a' (fresh). What does this pattern suggest?

options.label: A
options.text: Feeling sleepy means you should not exercise that day.

options.label: B
options.text: Only eating breakfast can make you feel fresh in the morning.

options.label: C
options.text: Sleeping for a longer stretch is likely to help you feel fresher the next day.

options.label: D
options.text: The amount of sleep does not affect how you feel the next day.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer: B. The item tests whether students can read a simple two-day pattern from their inquiry data. The other options probe common confusions between sleep, eating, and exercise as contributors to well-being.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can record and interpret personal sleep data and reason about why rest is necessary for the body.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing 'sleep does not affect how you feel' shows the student read the data but drew the opposite conclusion — a reasoning failure rather than a recall gap.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing 'only eating breakfast' shows the student confused the chapter's three pillars, attributing freshness to food rather than sleep.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 'feeling sleepy means no exercise' shows an overgeneralisation — the chapter presents exercise and rest as complementary, not opposed.

assessment_items.question_text: Your sleep record shows that on days when you played a lot, you slept better and felt fresher the next morning. How does this support the idea that eating well, exercising, and sleeping are all connected to each other?
look_for: Uses the personal sleep data pattern as evidence for a connection between exercise and quality of sleep.
Explains at least one link between the three pillars — e.g. exercise tires the body so it rests better; eating well gives energy for exercise; good sleep restores energy for the next day.
Shows that the three pillars work together rather than independently.
assessment_items.annotation: A strong response uses the sleep data as evidence and explains at least one connecting link between the three pillars. Partial credit for responses that state the connection without explaining the mechanism.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can draw a conclusion from their own recorded sleep data and connect adequate rest to overall well-being.

look_for: Uses the personal sleep data pattern as evidence for a connection between exercise and quality of sleep.
Explains at least one link between the three pillars — e.g. exercise tires the body so it rests better; eating well gives energy for exercise; good sleep restores energy for the next day.
Shows that the three pillars work together rather than independently.

assessment_items.question_text: A child feels confused and scared when an adult touches them in a way they do not like. The adult is someone the child knows well. What does this tell us?

options.label: A
options.text: An unsafe touch can come from someone known or from a stranger.

options.label: B
options.text: Because the adult is known, the touch must be safe.

options.label: C
options.text: The child is probably imagining the discomfort.

options.label: D
options.text: The child should not say anything because the adult might get upset.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer: B. The chapter explicitly states that an unsafe touch can come from someone known or a stranger. This is the section's key safety concept. Options A, C, and D represent common harmful beliefs that the section directly counters.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can classify physical interactions as safe or unsafe based on how the body and feelings respond.

competency.competency_text: Describes the basic safety needs and protection (health and hygiene, food, water, shelter, precautions, awareness of emergency situations, abuse, and unsafe situations) of humans, birds, and animals

what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing 'known adult means safe' is the most important misconception the section addresses — the student has not grasped that familiarity does not determine safety.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing 'say nothing' shows the student has absorbed a silencing belief rather than the empowerment message of the section.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing 'imagining it' shows the student has not accepted that a child's feelings of discomfort are valid indicators of an unsafe situation.

assessment_items.task: Think about a situation where someone's touch made you feel uneasy or confused. You do NOT have to share anything personal. Instead, write or draw what a child in that situation should do — step by step.
assessment_items.scaffold: Step 1: What should the child do first? Step 2: Who should the child tell? Step 3: What should the child remember about their right to feel safe?
format_of_output: OR a drawn sequence with labels
assessment_items.annotation: This task uses a fictional frame to protect students. Accept written steps, a drawn sequence, or a combination. Assess completeness of the three-step response (say No, move away, tell a trusted adult) and the affirmation of the right to safety. Do not require personal disclosure.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify appropriate responses to unsafe situations and articulate the right to bodily safety.

competency.competency_text: Describes the basic safety needs and protection (health and hygiene, food, water, shelter, precautions, awareness of emergency situations, abuse, and unsafe situations) of humans, birds, and animals

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student has internalised the three-step safety response and understands they have a right to feel safe regardless of who the person is.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The three steps guide the student without forcing personal disclosure. A strong response names a trusted adult in Step 2 and states the right to safety in Step 3.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: all three steps present, trusted adult named, explicit statement of the right to safety. Weak: only one or two steps, vague or no trusted adult named, no mention of the right to safety.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who prefer to draw their response should receive full credit if the drawn sequence communicates all three steps. Students may name any trusted adult relevant to their life.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Written steps or drawn sequence with labels
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Multiple formats allow all students to demonstrate understanding regardless of writing fluency, while keeping the output observable and assessable within a single session.

assessment_items.question_text: If there were no earthworms in the soil, what would most likely happen to a grain trying to grow? Give ONE specific reason for your answer.
expected_elements: States a consequence for the grain's growth — e.g. the grain would struggle to grow or the soil would be less fertile.
Gives a specific reason linked to the earthworm's role — e.g. earthworms loosen the soil or improve its quality, making it easier for roots to grow and absorb water and nutrients.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full credit for a consequence paired with a specific reason about the earthworm's function. Partial credit for stating a consequence without a reason, or naming the earthworm's role without stating a consequence.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can reason about the consequence of removing one contributor from an interdependent system and justify their thinking.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

expected_elements: States a consequence for the grain's growth — e.g. the grain would struggle to grow or the soil would be less fertile.
Gives a specific reason linked to the earthworm's role — e.g. earthworms loosen the soil or improve its quality, making it easier for roots to grow and absorb water and nutrients.

assessment_items.task: Design your lunch plate for today. Draw or write the foods you would put on it, making sure your plate is balanced and that you would finish everything — nothing wasted.
assessment_items.scaffold: My lunch plate will have: (List or draw the foods) I chose these foods because: (Write one reason) I will make sure I waste nothing by: (Write one action)
format_of_output: Drawing of a plate with labelled food items
OR a written list with explanations
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any culturally or regionally appropriate foods. Regional variation note: regionally varied food choices are all correct — the assessment criterion is balance and the no-waste plan, not specific food items. Award credit for a plate that shows variety (more than one food group) and a stated plan for finishing it.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can design a balanced meal plan that reflects understanding of nutritional variety and food-waste reduction.

competency.competency_text: Learns about basic social and behavioural norms, values, and dispositions that benefit our social and natural environments and that help our society function smoothly (using dustbins, standing in queues, conserving water, using public transportation, keeping one's environment clean, always helping others in need regardless of background)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can apply the concept of a balanced meal and the norm of not wasting food to a practical design task.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The three prompts check balance (variety of foods), justification (food choice reasoning), and the no-waste commitment (a specific action). Look for all three.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: multiple food types shown, clear reasoning for balance, specific no-waste action (e.g. 'I will take only what I can finish'). Weak: single food item, no reasoning, no waste-reduction plan.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Drawing and writing are equally valid. All regional foods are acceptable. Students with limited writing ability may be credited fully for a labelled drawing.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Drawing with labels or written list with explanation
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Both formats produce an observable, collectable output that demonstrates the same understanding, ensuring access for all learners.

assessment_items.task: Choose THREE habits from this list: wake up early, yoga and exercises, eat a balanced diet on time, exercise and play, less use of TV and mobile, read a book, sleep peacefully. For each habit, write WHY it helps keep you happy and healthy.
assessment_items.scaffold: Habit 1: ___ — This helps me because: Habit 2: ___ — This helps me because: Habit 3: ___ — This helps me because:
format_of_output: OR a drawn plan with written labels and reasons
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any three habits from the list. Assess the quality of the 'because' reasoning — does it connect the habit to a specific benefit for the body or mind? Reasons that simply repeat the habit name (e.g. 'sleeping helps because you sleep') are weak. Reasons that describe a specific effect (e.g. 'sleeping well helps my body repair so I feel fresh') are strong.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify and commit to specific personal habits that support physical and emotional well-being.

competency.competency_text: Learns about basic social and behavioural norms, values, and dispositions that benefit our social and natural environments and that help our society function smoothly (using dustbins, standing in queues, conserving water, using public transportation, keeping one's environment clean, always helping others in need regardless of background)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Whether the student can articulate a specific, reasoned link between a chosen habit and its benefit for physical or emotional well-being — moving beyond recall to evaluative justification.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Each row prompts a choice and a reason. A complete response has three distinct habits and three distinct reasons. Look for specificity in the 'because' clause.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: three distinct habits chosen, each with a specific, distinct benefit explained. Weak: habits named without reasons, or reasons that simply restate the habit.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students may draw a habit plan with labels and brief written reasons. Students who cannot write full sentences may use key words alongside a drawing for partial credit.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Written three-habit plan with reasons, or drawn plan with labels and reasons
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The open format allows personalisation — students commit to habits that are achievable in their own lives — while the 'because' requirement ensures the response is evaluative, not merely a list.
